Jagrat Fleet Systems: Ranking the Q4 Backlog

A short teaching case on value versus effort

1. Bengaluru, 1 October 2026

Radhika Iyer, VP of Product at Jagrat Fleet Systems, opened the board deck template and felt the familiar tightness in her chest. In eight days she would fly to Gurugram to present the fourth-quarter roadmap, and the board had been blunt after the last review: fewer promises, and a roadmap showing, item by item, why each feature earned its place. Outside her window on Outer Ring Road, October traffic was already thickening with the trucks and vans of her company's business — the run-up to the festive season, when parcel volumes climb by a third before Diwali. Her engineering capacity would not climb with them. She had eight credible asks from four directions, roughly fifty-one engineer-weeks of work, and about thirty-six weeks to spend. Something would not get built, and whoever missed out would want to know why.

2. The company

Jagrat Fleet Systems sold fleet-telematics and delivery-operations software — GPS tracking, route optimisation, driver scorecards, proof-of-delivery capture — to trucking and last-mile logistics companies across India. Founded in 2019, it had grown to ₹38 crore in annual recurring revenue by mid-2026, with roughly ninety paying customers from regional trucking fleets to national courier networks. It competed against LogiNext, Locus and FarEye, and its customers moved freight for shippers like Ecom Express, DTDC and Mahindra Logistics. The product integrated with India's GST e-way bill system and, increasingly, FASTag toll data. Engineering was split between a platform pod of three in Bengaluru and a delivery pod of two in Pune; a designer worked from Berlin, a data scientist from Toronto, a customer-success lead ran Asia-Pacific and Gulf accounts from Singapore, and a sales head covered North America from New Jersey. The company had raised its Series B eighteen months earlier on a growth story; the board now wanted evidence that growth was being spent deliberately.

3. The situation

The backlog had grown noisy because every function had a legitimate claim on it. Vikram Nair, the Bengaluru engineering lead, had spent September fielding two production incidents where the routing engine buckled under load, and wanted a rewrite before festive volumes hit. Farah Rahman, running customer success from Singapore, had spent the month on calls with three unhappy accounts — including Junoon Freight DMCC, a large Dubai-based transport operator and Jagrat's biggest Gulf customer — whose drivers submitted blurry proof-of-delivery photos and whose dispatchers no longer trusted the app's ETA numbers. Derek Wallace, the New Jersey-based sales head, was chasing two North American prospects who had asked, almost in the same words, for a "control tower" dashboard with predictive arrival times before they would sign; he believed the deals were worth ₹3.2 crore combined. Arjun Mehta, the data scientist in Toronto, had spent the summer building a machine-learning routing model and wanted engineering time to wire it into the live product. Lena Hoffmann, the Berlin-based designer, had research showing new drivers abandoned onboarding at a rate that cost support hours. Radhika had sat in on calls at 7 a.m., 1 p.m. and 9 p.m. Bengaluru time to hear each case in its own zone, and came away convinced everyone was arguing sincerely — and that "value" meant something different depending on where you sat.

4. The people

  • Vikram Nair, Engineering Lead, Bengaluru. Owns the routing engine that broke twice in September. Wants a rewrite before peak season; fears a third outage in the Diwali fortnight could trigger SLA penalties across the trucking book.
  • Farah Rahman, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Manages Asia-Pacific and Gulf accounts, including Junoon Freight DMCC. Measures value in renewal risk; three accounts worth ₹65 lakh ARR are due for Q1 renewal and unhappy about proof-of-delivery and ETA accuracy.
  • Derek Wallace, Sales Head, North America, New Jersey. Measures value in new bookings. Argues the predictive dashboard is the only thing between Jagrat and two logo wins that would diversify it beyond India.
  • Lena Hoffmann, Product Designer, Berlin, alongside Arjun Mehta, Data Scientist, Toronto. Lena wants the driver-app redesign shipped to cut onboarding drop-off; Arjun wants his routing model integrated after three idle months of engineering effort.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 lists the eight items with Radhika's estimate of value against effort. The total ask — fifty-one engineer-weeks — exceeds the roughly thirty-six the two pods can realistically deliver (Exhibit 3). Value is not proportional to effort: the cheapest item, the proof-of-delivery fix, protects nearly as much revenue as the costliest item promises to create, at a fifth of the time.

Plotting the same items on a value-effort grid, Exhibit 2, makes the choice easier to see. The upper-right "big bets" quadrant holds both the routing rewrite and the control-tower dashboard — but only one protects revenue the company already has. The upper-left quick-wins quadrant holds exactly one item: Farah's fix.

Exhibit 3 sets the backlog against actual pod capacity, and against how much revenue was already at risk versus merely hoped for — a rupee of ARR she might lose in December was not the same kind of rupee as a rupee of pipeline Derek might close in March.

Sixty percent allocatable reflects the historical split between roadmap work and on-call, incidents and configuration.

6. The options

  • Option A — Protect the base, then rebuild. Fund the quick win (3), compliance (6), FASTag (7) and localisation (8) in full — thirteen weeks — then commit the remaining twenty-three to a scoped routing rewrite (1). Upside: resolves escalations on ₹2.6 crore of renewals, including Junoon Freight DMCC, before the festive surge, and cuts outage risk. Cost: the dashboard and the ML model wait until Q1, disappointing Derek and Arjun.
  • Option B — Chase the big bet. Commit fourteen weeks to the predictive dashboard, two to compliance, and twenty to a partial POD/ETA fix and UX redesign. Upside: a credible shot at ₹3.2 crore in new bookings and a growth story for the board. Cost: the routing engine goes unrebuilt into peak season; Junoon Freight DMCC and other escalations stay partly resolved, carrying renewal risk into Q1.
  • Option C — Spread it across everyone. Allocate proportional slices of the thirty-six weeks across all five major asks. Upside: avoids an uncomfortable conversation this quarter. Cost: nothing reaches production finished; the engine stays fragile, escalations stay open, the dashboard stays half-built — five bars of "in progress," the outcome the board had already warned against.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, which quadrant does each item fall into, and what does that suggest about sequencing?
  2. Vikram, Farah, Derek and Lena each define "value" differently. What explains each definition, and whose should carry the most weight this quarter?
  3. Arjun has already spent three months building the ML routing model. Should that sunk effort change how much weight item 5 gets, or is it irrelevant to the decision now?
  4. Given thirty-six effective engineer-weeks and the deadline, which items should Radhika commit to, and what would she tell whichever stakeholder she declines?

8. A note for the learner

Value-versus-effort is the simplest prioritisation lens in product management: it forces two separate judgements — how much this is worth, and how much it costs to get it — instead of one blended gut feeling. Most backlog arguments, like this one, are really disagreements about which axis matters more, dressed up as disagreements about the whole ranking. Vikram, Farah, Derek and Lena are not wrong about their own numbers; they reason from different vantage points on the same grid.

A well-reasoned answer treats the two axes with different levels of trust. Effort estimates in engineer-weeks are reasonably solid, produced by Radhika's own teams. Value estimates are not: an escalation already happening (item 3) is a fact; a pipeline not yet signed (item 4) is a forecast; a model not yet tested on live drivers (item 5) is a hope. The framework does not say to ignore hopes and forecasts — it says to discount them relative to facts, and to be honest about which is which.

On that reasoning, Option A is the defensible path: it spends the cheap, high-confidence quick win first, satisfies the one non-negotiable compliance item, and puts remaining capacity into the item protecting revenue already booked, ahead of the season when losing it would cost most. It declines, for now, the two most speculative items — not because Derek's ambition or Arjun's model is worthless, but because neither has earned the fourteen or eight weeks a big bet demands from a thirty-six-week quarter. What Radhika owes them is not "no" but "not yet, and here is what would change my mind" — a signed pilot customer, or a validated fuel-savings result on a small fleet subset. Option C, giving everyone a slice, is what the framework rules out most clearly: spreading thirty-six weeks across fifty-one weeks of asks guarantees nothing finishes — the one outcome the board had already ruled out.

Kaarigar Craft Exchange: The Ledger, the Buyer and the Board

An extended case on choosing what to build when value and effort are both contested

1. Jaipur, Thursday 8 October 2026, 11.40 p.m.

The Malviya Nagar office had emptied hours earlier, and Ishani Deshmukh had the floor to herself but for the guard, who had twice come up to ask whether she wanted the air-conditioning kept running. On her screen were three versions of the same slide, each the half-year roadmap for Kaarigar Craft Exchange. Each was defensible. No two agreed on a single line item.

On Monday the executive team would lock the roadmap for November through April; on Wednesday 15 October the founder, Rohit Sabharwal, would take it to the board alongside the first serious Series C conversation. After that there was no room to change her mind: the deck came from the roadmap, and the roadmap from a backlog holding seventy-three engineer-weeks of asks against roughly forty-one weeks of capacity.

What kept her at her desk was not the shortfall; she had cut backlogs before. It was that two of the numbers she had presented in August — the ones the plan rested on — had since been contradicted by her own engineers, and she was no longer confident that the framing she had taught the company, ranking every item by the value it created against the effort it cost, pointed at the right question.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2023

Kaarigar Craft Exchange was founded in Jaipur in 2019 by Rohit Sabharwal, a former export-house merchandiser, and Sandeep Rao, an engineer. It was a cross-border marketplace: some 6,400 artisan units across Jaipur, Moradabad, Bhadohi, Saharanpur and Channapatna, selling home furnishings, brassware, rugs and wooden goods to wholesale buyers in the Gulf, Europe and North America. It took seven to nine per cent on transacted value, plus a documentation fee. In the year to March 2026 it recorded ₹310 crore of gross merchandise value and ₹26 crore of net revenue, and lost ₹19 crore doing it.

The decision that shaped everything afterwards was taken in late 2023. Buyers in Dubai and Rotterdam paid in dirhams and euros, artisans in Bhadohi needed rupees within a fortnight, and the payment providers then available either would not hold funds in escrow against inspection milestones or charged in a way that ate the commission outright. Sandeep argued that Kaarigar should build its own settlement ledger: a double-entry system holding buyer funds, releasing them against inspection and shipment events, booking the currency conversion and generating the paperwork Indian exporters must file. Rohit agreed. Ten months and ₹4 crore later, it had a ledger that worked.

It worked for one currency pair, one shipment per purchase order, and a tenth of today's volume. Every capability wanted since — split shipments, partial refunds, consolidated containers, reconciliation of export bills against inward remittance — had been bolted to its side. By 2026 the ledger constrained the product, the finance team, and what Ishani could promise.

3. The industry

India's handicrafts and home-furnishing exports were fragmented, cyclical and government-attended. The Export Promotion Council for Handicrafts published the sector numbers; the Directorate General of Foreign Trade set the RoDTEP remission rates many small exporters treated as their margin; customs filings ran through ICEGATE; and the Reserve Bank of India's export data processing system tracked whether every shipping bill was matched by an inward remittance, with overdue bills raised in writing by the bank.

Kaarigar sat between several kinds of competitor. IndiaMART and Udaan had scale in domestic wholesale discovery; Amazon Global Selling and Etsy pulled the better-organised artisan units straight to Western consumers; Flipkart's Samarth programme and the government-backed ONDC network courted the same clusters with domestic demand. And a well-funded Bengaluru rival, Kashida Handloom Exchange, had spent 2026 buying share with zero commission for first-year sellers and a seller app in seven languages.

Kaarigar's exposure was global in an uncomfortable way. Fifty-eight per cent of GMV came from twelve buying groups, the largest being Al Qasba Home Trading LLC, a Dubai wholesaler supplying hotel groups and retail chains across the Gulf. European buyers ordered against a Christmas calendar, so the decisive shipping window ran from January to March, not around Diwali. And the rupee's drift against the dollar made the ledger's single-currency assumptions more visibly wrong each month.

4. The situation in detail

In March 2026, after three large orders were delayed by manual reconciliation, leadership agreed in principle that the ledger had to be re-architected. No date was set. In April, sales operations redefined the CRM pipeline stages, a detail that would matter later.

In June, Al Qasba's head of sourcing told Meghna Iyengar, Kaarigar's customer-success lead in Singapore, that it would consolidate its Indian buying onto fewer platforms in 2027, and needed a request-for-quotation and sampling workflow — one specification to nine artisan units, costed samples back, a split order against a single container. Its memorandum came up for renewal on 30 November.

In July, Dr Nikhil Varma, the data scientist in Toronto, demonstrated a catalogue-enrichment model that read artisan photographs, extracted dimensions and materials, removed backgrounds and generated structured attributes. On 4,000 held-out listings it improved search relevance by a margin he characterised as an eleven per cent lift in buyer conversion. In August, Ishani compiled the backlog into one ranked list with estimated value and effort (Exhibit 1), plotted it (Exhibit 2), and presented it. Rohit called it "the first roadmap I could actually defend."

In September, three things went wrong with that list. Sandeep, uneasy about the ledger estimate, put two engineers on a fortnight of discovery spikes; the re-estimate came back at thirty-four engineer-weeks rather than twenty-two, and said the work could not usefully be split below about twenty (Exhibit 3). Second, his team found Nikhil's model could not be served at production latency without an image pipeline nobody had costed. Third, Meghna's team surveyed buyers who had not reordered (Exhibit 4); the top reason was not search, not payments and not paperwork, but lead time from order to shipment — which Kaarigar did not control and had no backlog item for.

On 2 October, Prakash Ranganathan, the finance controller, forwarded a letter from the authorised dealer bank listing 214 shipping bills, worth ₹31 crore, for which inward remittance had not been matched. Most were clerical. All had to be regularised, and by hand that would take the finance team into January.

5. The people

  • Ishani Deshmukh, VP Product, Jaipur. Joined in 2024 from a Bengaluru grocery marketplace. Introduced the value-versus-effort discipline of the August plan, and is most publicly committed to it. Believes the ledger must be rebuilt. Has not said aloud that she doubts the company survives two quarters of a roadmap with nothing on it a buyer can see.
  • Rohit Sabharwal, Founder and CEO, Jaipur and Delhi. Needs a Series C in the first half of 2027 and believes the story that raises it is a network story: ONDC, seller growth, GMV. The board measures him on GMV, not gross margin. Has not told the team that one prospective investor has twice asked why the take rate keeps falling.
  • Sandeep Rao, Co-founder and Head of Engineering, Hyderabad. Built the 2023 ledger and is now its loudest critic. Calls every other item a "rope bridge over the same ravine," and wants the rewrite funded whole or not at all. Does not mention that it would also retire the on-call burden that has cost him two senior engineers this year.
  • Meghna Iyengar, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Owns the Gulf and South-East Asia book, including Al Qasba Home Trading LLC (₹41 crore GMV in FY26). Wants the RFQ workflow before the 30 November renewal. Is privately unsure Al Qasba would actually leave, and has not said her contact there has changed twice in a year.
  • Greg Pilato, Head of Sales, North America, New Jersey. Has two large prospects — a hospitality supply group and a furnishings retailer — both wanting a compliance pack of US product-safety documentation and timber-sourcing certificates. Values the pair at ₹6.5 crore of GMV in year one. His variable pay is weighted to new logos. Does not volunteer that neither has moved past a second meeting.
  • Suraj Yadav, Head of Supply, Moradabad. Owns artisan onboarding, and watches Kashida Handloom Exchange take sellers with a better regional-language app and faster payouts. Measures himself in active sellers, a metric that rises on joining and falls slowly on going quiet, which flatters.
  • Dr Nikhil Varma, Data Scientist, Toronto. Six months into a two-year contract; the enrichment model is his whole visible output. Argues the eleven per cent is conservative. Has not run it against Gulf buyers' search behaviour, which differs sharply from the European pattern he tested on.
  • Annika Roth, Product Designer, Berlin. The only person who has sat with both artisans in Saharanpur and buyers in Rotterdam. Argues the backlog is written in the language of internal teams, not of either customer. The least powerful voice in the room, and she knows it.
  • Prakash Ranganathan, Finance Controller, Jaipur. Has a bank letter, a statutory obligation and four staff. Will argue about how the reconciliation happens, not whether.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the list Ishani presented in August: nine items, each with a champion, a value in whatever unit that champion found natural, and an effort estimate.

Exhibit 3 is what Sandeep's team produced in September. It disagrees with Exhibit 1 on four rows, and in two the direction surprised everyone.

Exhibit 4 is the buyer survey, sent to 340 buyers who transacted once in FY26 and did not return; sixty-one replied. It is the only direct evidence of what buyers say, and it points where the backlog does not go.

7. Voices

Sandeep Rao, engineering review, 24 September"Every quarter we agree the ledger is the problem and every quarter we fund something we can show a customer instead. Thirty-four weeks is not a negotiating position. Give me twenty and I build two-thirds of a ledger, which is worth less than none of one."
Greg Pilato, email to Rohit and Ishani, 28 September"Seven weeks. Sandeep's own number, not mine. Seven weeks for the only item here that brings in a customer who has never paid us anything. I am not asking to jump the queue. I am asking why the cheapest revenue item on the board sits below a Hindi keyboard."
Suraj Yadav, internal chat, 29 September"Greg, respectfully — the 'Hindi keyboard' is 2,800 units in Moradabad and Saharanpur reconciling payouts by sending me WhatsApp photographs of a passbook. Kashida pays them in four days. We pay in eleven and cannot say why."
Meghna Iyengar, call notes, 1 October"Al Qasba will not say they are leaving. They will place the spring order through two platforms instead of one and call it a pilot. By the time it shows in our numbers it will be April."
Annika Roth, comment on the roadmap document, 3 October"Nine items, and eight are named after the team that wants them. Exhibit 4 says buyers complain about lead time. Nobody has asked whether any of this software changes a lead time."
Rohit Sabharwal, to Ishani, 6 October"I can raise on a broken ledger. I cannot raise on a flat GMV chart. Tell me which of these moves the chart by March."
Prakash Ranganathan, email, 7 October"The 214 bills are not a product decision. They will be regularised. The only question is whether that is five weeks of engineering or four accountants working through December and January, during which they will not close the books."

8. The options as Ishani sees them

  • A. Fund the ledger whole. Thirty-four weeks to item 1, five to item 9, two left over. The constraint goes and every later item gets cheaper. The cost is six months in which no buyer and no seller sees anything new, Al Qasba renews on a promise or not at all, and the GMV chart stays flat through the Series C conversation.
  • B. Protect the biggest account. Items 2 (nine weeks), 7 (four), 8 (three), 9 (five) and 4 (seven) — twenty-eight weeks, leaving thirteen for a partial ledger start Sandeep says is worth nothing. Defends ₹41 crore of GMV, gives Greg his shot, and keeps the ledger where it is for another year.
  • C. Build the growth story. ONDC (fifteen), enrichment (sixteen), EDPMS (five) — thirty-six weeks, and a deck with a new demand channel and an AI capability in it. Both value claims are modelled rather than observed, and neither has a buyer waiting.
  • D. Defend the supply side. Seller app (six), payout dashboard (three), EDPMS (five), landed cost (four), eighteen weeks toward the ledger. Answers Kashida's poaching and the eleven-day payout, but those eighteen weeks buy, on Sandeep's own account, an unfinished ledger.

She had written all four on the whiteboard and, at about ten, three questions underneath that she could not answer. Whether "the ledger" was one item or three, and whether thirty-four weeks was indivisible because it truly was or because the man estimating it wanted it funded whole. Whether value accruing to an artisan in Saharanpur belonged on the same axis as value accruing to the take rate. And whether any of the nine items touched the twenty-seven buyers in Exhibit 4 who had left over lead time — a number from a survey that listed lead time first and excluded every buyer who mattered most.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Monday's meeting was at nine; the roadmap locked there went into Tuesday's board pack. Forty-one engineer-weeks was not negotiable before February: the hiring freeze held but for one backfill, and Rohit had declined a Pune agency contract because the Series C conversation would go badly if burn rose in the same quarter. The 214 bills had to be regularised by the end of December one way or another. The Al Qasba memorandum expired on 30 November. The European shipping window opened in January, so anything meant to affect spring orders had to be live by then. And the take rate had fallen from 8.4 to 7.1 per cent over five quarters — addressed by no item on the list, noticed twice by an investor.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Plot the nine items twice, once with the August numbers and once with the September re-estimates. Which change quadrant, and what does that fragility say about the tool?
  2. The nine value claims in Exhibit 1 use six different units. What would it take to put them on one axis honestly, and what is lost in the conversion?
  3. Exhibits 4 and 5 point in opposite directions about who Kaarigar should build for. How was each produced, and how much weight does each deserve?
  4. Sandeep says the ledger cannot usefully be split below twenty weeks. What would you need to believe that, and what if you could not get it?
  5. Items 5 and 8 create most of their value for artisans, not for Kaarigar's near-term revenue. On what basis, if any, should that value sit on the same grid as Greg's pipeline?
  6. What should Ishani put on the whiteboard at nine on Monday, what should she stop believing first, and what would she say to the board on Wednesday?

It was past one. Ishani had a version of the slide in which the ledger consumed the half-year and one in which it did not appear at all, and could defend either in a way Rohit would accept and Sandeep would not. On the desk lay Prakash's printout, which decided five of the forty-one weeks for her, and a sticky note in Annika's hand from a July workshop: whose week is it? She turned off the monitor without saving any of the three.

Value versus Effort

The 2×2 that every other prioritisation framework is quietly a variation of — and the four or five judgements it hides inside its two innocent-looking axes.

1. A Tuesday in Pune

On Tuesday 14 July 2026, Aditi Bhave sat in a glass-walled room on the third floor of an office park in Baner, Pune, looking at a whiteboard with nine sticky notes on it and a number written in the corner: 66. Aditi was the senior product manager for the order-management module at Lavanika Commerce Cloud, a company that sold back-office software to direct-to-consumer brands — the unglamorous plumbing that takes an order placed on a brand's website, decides which warehouse should ship it, prints the label, and tells the customer where the parcel is. Lavanika had 340 paying brands, annual recurring revenue of ₹58 crore, and, for the module Aditi owned, exactly one engineering squad: six engineers, one designer, one QA analyst.

The 66 was the number of engineer-weeks the squad had between that Tuesday and the code freeze on 28 September, eleven weeks later. Lavanika froze in late September because its customers sold festive-season goods and would not tolerate a deployment anywhere near Dussehra or Diwali. Whatever did not ship by the freeze would not ship until January. The nine sticky notes represented roughly 140 engineer-weeks of requests. Aditi had to decide what 66 weeks' worth of them would be.

The requests had arrived from every direction. The head of sales wanted a returns-management workflow, because two enterprise prospects worth a combined ₹1.9 crore of new ARR had named it as a gap. The largest existing customer, a footwear brand with ₹240 crore of GMV flowing through Lavanika, had asked for multi-warehouse split shipments and had a renewal due in November. Support had escalated a bug-adjacent nuisance — an order-search screen that timed out for brands with more than two lakh orders — which generated about forty tickets a month. The CTO wanted a fortnight spent replacing the ageing webhook delivery service before it fell over under festive load. And the CEO, returning from a conference, had asked whether Lavanika should build an AI assistant that answered operations questions in plain language, because three competitors had announced one.

Aditi could not do all of it and she knew that arguing about which item was most important, item by item, would consume the week and end wherever the loudest voice wanted it to end. What she needed was a way to convert nine incommensurable arguments into one ordered list, together with a defensible account of why that order and not another. That is precisely the job the value-versus-effort matrix was invented to do — and, as she would discover by Thursday, precisely the job it does only if you are honest about what you are putting into it.

2. The idea, stated precisely

The value-versus-effort matrix is a decision aid in which every candidate piece of work is placed on two axes — an estimate of the value it is expected to create, and an estimate of the effort it will cost to deliver — and the work is then sequenced so that the items producing the most value per unit of effort come first. Value means the expected contribution to a stated outcome within a stated time horizon: revenue retained, revenue won, cost avoided, risk removed, a behaviour changed. Effort means the total cost to reach a shippable state — design, engineering, testing, migration, documentation, enablement — not merely the hours a developer spends typing. The output is not a picture. The output is an order.

The problem it was invented to solve is older than software. In the late 1960s and 1970s, the Japanese quality movement associated with Kaoru Ishikawa and the spread of quality-control circles gave managers a family of simple graphical aids for choosing among improvement projects, the prioritisation matrix among them. In parallel, the Boston Consulting Group's growth–share matrix of 1970 taught a generation of managers to place competing claims on capital in a two-by-two and argue about the placement rather than the conclusion. Both traditions rest on a far older piece of arithmetic: when a fixed budget must be spread across projects of differing cost and differing return, ordering by ratio of return to cost gets you close to the best achievable portfolio. Software teams inherited the device through Lean and Agile practice in the 2000s, where it appears as the impact–effort matrix, and everything that came later — RICE, weighted scoring, WSJF, Kano-informed ranking — is an attempt to make one of its two axes less crude.

The sentence Aditi could say in a meeting without sounding glib: “We are not ranking these by how much we want them. We are ranking them by how much outcome each one buys per engineer-week, and then we are drawing a line where the squad's capacity runs out.”

3. How it actually works

Practitioners usually describe the mechanic as three steps — estimate value, estimate effort, plot — and in doing so skip the four judgements that determine the answer. The honest version has seven.

First, fix the outcome and the horizon. Value is meaningless as a free-floating quantity; it is always value towards something, by when. Aditi's team wrote at the top of the whiteboard: “Outcome: net revenue retention above 108% for FY27, and ₹4 crore of new ARR closed by March.” That single line does more prioritisation work than the rest of the exercise, because it tells you that a delightful improvement with no bearing on retention or on closing deals is, for this quarter, worth close to zero.

Second, normalise the items. A list containing “fix the order-search timeout” (four days) and “build an AI operations assistant” (an open-ended programme) cannot be ranked, because the second item is not one decision but twenty. Aditi split the AI assistant into a three-week read-only prototype answering five specific questions, and left the rest unestimated. Items should be of roughly comparable size — within perhaps a factor of four — before they go on the same grid.

Third, estimate value against the stated outcome, using a scale everyone applies the same way. Lavanika used a 1–10 scale anchored with examples: a 9 meant “directly protects or wins more than ₹1 crore of ARR”; a 3 meant “measurably improves the experience of a minority of customers with no near-term revenue consequence”. Anchoring matters more than the scale's granularity.

Fourth, estimate effort as cost-to-done. The engineering lead, Karthik Nair, gave estimates in engineer-weeks that included QA and migration. For the split-shipment work he added three weeks for backfilling existing orders — a cost the product side had not been counting.

Fifth, compute the ratio of value to effort for every item, and sort descending. This, not the quadrant, is the decision rule. Sixth, fill capacity down the sorted list until the budget is exhausted, and draw the line. Seventh, override the order deliberately and in writing where dependencies, contractual commitments or risk demand it — and record each override, because a list of overrides is the most useful artefact the exercise produces.

The diagonals are the part most readers have never been shown. The familiar version of this tool divides the plane into four boxes — quick wins, big bets, fill-ins, money pits — using two arbitrary midpoints. But the midpoints carry no information: they are wherever someone drew them. What carries information is the slope of the line from the origin through each point, because that slope is the value-per-unit-effort ratio. Two items in the same quadrant can differ threefold in ratio, and two items in different quadrants can be exactly equivalent. The quadrant is a vocabulary for conversation; the diagonal is the decision.

4. The arithmetic, line by line

Here is the full table Aditi's team built on the Wednesday. Value is the 1–10 anchored score; effort is engineer-weeks to done; ratio is value divided by effort, to two decimals; the cumulative column fills the 66-week budget down the sorted order.

Read the table slowly, because the surprise is in it. If Aditi had ranked by value alone — the instinct almost every stakeholder has — she would have started with B (9) and C (8), spent thirty of her sixty-six weeks on those two, and delivered five items. Ranking by ratio delivers seven items and 42 points of value against 54 weeks. Ranking by value alone delivers 40 points against 63 weeks. The ratio ordering is about 22% more productive per week, and the gap comes entirely from the cheap, unglamorous items at the top — the SLA view and the search fix — that nobody would have argued for in a room.

The second pass: one input changes

On Thursday, Karthik came back from a session with the platform team. The returns workflow, item C, could reuse a state machine another squad had already built for exchanges. His estimate fell from 18 engineer-weeks to 9. At the same time, a call with the footwear customer revealed that split shipments were contractually required for their renewal, not merely desired, which pushed B's value from 9 to 10; and the customer's catalogue structure added 4 weeks of work, taking B from 12 to 16.

This is the most instructive moment in the whole exercise, and it is why good programmes make students prioritise a deliberately noisy backlog rather than a tidy one. Two ordinary pieces of new information — a reusable component and a contract clause — reordered the list. Nothing about the strategy changed. Nothing about customer needs changed. What changed were two estimates, and estimates are the softest part of the machine. A practitioner who understands the tool treats the ranking as a live function of its inputs and asks, of every ordering, “which single estimate, if wrong, would change this?” A practitioner who merely uses the vocabulary treats Wednesday's list as a decision and defends it on Thursday.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Value is a property of a bet, not of a feature

“The returns workflow is worth 8” is shorthand for “if we ship a returns workflow of roughly this scope by September, we expect it to unlock two deals worth ₹1.9 crore, and we are moderately confident of that.” Every value score conceals a forecast and a confidence level. When a stakeholder says a feature is high-value, the productive next question is never “why?” but “worth what, to whom, by when, and how sure are you?” Written that way, half the disagreements in the room dissolve, because the parties discover they were forecasting different things.

Effort is cost-to-done, and the long tail is where budgets die

Development is frequently the smaller half. Lavanika's returns workflow needed a migration script for six lakh historical orders, a change to the customer-facing help centre, a training session for the twelve-person support team, and a pricing decision about whether returns sat in the base plan. Teams that estimate only the coding consistently underestimate by forty to sixty per cent, and — because the underestimate is proportionally worse for complex items — systematically bias the ranking towards big, ambitious work. The bias runs in the direction people already want to go, which is what makes it dangerous.

The quadrants are a vocabulary; the diagonal is the rule

Calling something a “quick win” or a “money pit” helps a room converse, and there is genuine value in a shared label. But the four boxes depend on where the midlines are drawn, and nobody draws them from evidence. If you find yourself arguing about whether an item is in the top-right or bottom-right box, you are arguing about a line that carries no information. Compute the ratio instead and the argument becomes about the two numbers, which is where it belongs.

Uncertainty is not the same as low value

A speculative item with a wide range of possible outcomes will be scored low by a cautious team and high by an optimistic one, and the matrix cannot arbitrate. The clean fix is to separate the two ideas: score the value you would expect if the bet works, then multiply by a confidence factor between 0 and 1. That decomposition is exactly the move RICE makes — reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort — and understanding it as a refinement of this 2×2 rather than a different framework is the difference between knowing prioritisation and knowing acronyms.

The ratio rule is a greedy heuristic, not an optimum

Ordering by value-per-unit-cost is the standard approximation to what mathematicians call the knapsack problem, and it is provably near-optimal only when items are small relative to the budget. When a single item consumes half your capacity, greedy ordering can be beaten: there are cases where skipping the top-ranked item lets you fit two others whose combined value is higher. With 66 weeks and a largest item of 18, Lavanika's list was safely in the regime where the heuristic works. A team with 12 weeks and a 10-week item is not, and should enumerate the handful of feasible combinations by hand.

Dependencies and enablers break the ordering

The webhook rebuild scored 4 for value in its own right. But if the split-shipment feature would generate three times the webhook traffic and the old service was already near its limit, then part of B's value is contingent on D shipping first, and D's true value is partly derived from B's. Enabling work is chronically under-ranked by this tool because its value shows up on someone else's row. The practical fix is to score the pair as a bundle when the dependency is hard, and to note the dependency explicitly when it is soft.

The matrix cannot tell you whether the strategy is right

It ranks candidates against a stated outcome; it is silent on whether that outcome is the one to pursue, and it can only rank what someone thought to write on a sticky note. The most valuable thing Lavanika could have done in FY27 might not have been on the whiteboard at all. Nor does it handle non-negotiables: a feature required by law, or by a signed contract, does not get ranked, it gets scheduled — which is the gap MoSCoW's “must have” category exists to fill.

It says nothing about portfolio balance

Pure ratio ordering will happily produce a quarter made entirely of small improvements, because small items tend to have attractive ratios. A year of that and the product has no new capability and the team has no new skills. Mature teams run the ratio ordering and then apply an explicit allocation — say, 70% ranked work, 20% platform health, 10% exploration — as a constraint layered on top, rather than pretending the constraint falls out of the arithmetic.

6. How the picture changes by product type and stage

In consumer products, value is usually estimated from reach and measured behaviour: how many users touch this surface, and what does a comparable past change suggest about conversion or retention? The estimates are noisy but they are at least empirical, and they can be checked afterwards with an experiment. In B2B software like Lavanika's, reach is small and concentrated — nine of the 340 brands generate a third of the revenue — so value collapses into account-specific reasoning, and the honest score is often “this protects ₹4 crore of renewal.” The risk in B2B is that the loudest account becomes the strategy; the corrective is to ask how many other accounts would use the same capability, and to require an answer with a number in it.

In marketplaces and platforms the tool needs surgery, because value accrues to two different populations and a feature can be strongly positive for one and negative for the other. A change that reduces seller listing friction may raise catalogue volume and lower catalogue quality. Practitioners who work on two-sided products typically score value twice — once per side — and then argue explicitly about which side is currently the constraint on growth, because the answer determines which score should dominate. Collapsing that into one number hides the only interesting question.

Stage matters as much as type. In an eight-person startup, effort estimates are accurate because the estimator will do the work, and value estimates are wild because there is no history; the matrix is mostly useful for exposing that three of five items serve no current outcome. In a company of Lavanika's size, effort estimates degrade — cross-team dependencies, release trains, compliance review — while value estimates improve, because there are enough customers and enough past releases to reason from. In a very large organisation the exercise often shifts from ranking features to ranking initiatives across teams, at which point the effort axis must be denominated in something comparable across squads, usually money or team-quarters rather than engineer-weeks.

7. Common mistakes and their cheapest diagnostics

Everything scores 8 or 9

Symptom: the value column has almost no spread, and the ranking is driven entirely by effort. Misunderstanding: participants are scoring how much they want the item rather than its contribution to the stated outcome, and nobody wants to mark their own request a 3. Diagnostic: force-rank instead of scoring. Ask the group to place the items in a single line from most to least valuable with no ties permitted. Compression vanishes immediately, because relative judgements are easier and more honest than absolute ones.

The optimist estimates the effort

Symptom: items consistently ship at two to three times their estimate, and the pattern is worse for the ambitious items. Misunderstanding: the estimate was for the happy path of the coding, produced by the person most excited about the work. Diagnostic: compare the last two quarters' estimates against actuals and compute a per-team multiplier. Lavanika's was 1.6. Applying a known multiplier is not pessimism; it is calibration, and it changes rankings because it penalises large items proportionally more.

Quadrant theatre

Symptom: a beautifully drawn matrix appears in the deck, and the roadmap that follows is the one the most senior person in the room wanted before the workshop. Misunderstanding: the tool was treated as a presentation format rather than a decision rule. Diagnostic: ask what the matrix changed. If no item moved position and nothing was cut, the exercise produced no information and the time would have been better spent on the estimates.

The grid is drawn once and never revisited

Symptom: six weeks into the quarter, the team is still building item 7 although the customer who requested it has churned. Misunderstanding: the ranking was taken as a commitment rather than as the current best reading of live inputs. Diagnostic: a standing fortnightly question — “which estimate on this list have we learned something about since we made it?” Ten minutes, and it is the single highest-return meeting most teams are not holding.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the exercise takes a team about three hours across two sessions and produces four things. First, an explicit outcome statement at the top of the sheet, so that value is anchored to something. Second, a table with two estimated columns, a computed ratio, and a cumulative-effort line that makes the cut visible rather than debatable. Third, a short, written list of deliberate overrides — “D moves above H despite a lower ratio because B depends on it” — which is the record that lets a future reader reconstruct the reasoning. Fourth, a named list of the two or three estimates the ranking is most sensitive to, each with an owner and a date by which it will be tightened. Nobody leaves the room believing the numbers are true. Everybody leaves knowing what would have to change for the plan to change, which is a far more durable form of agreement.

9. What Aditi decided

On Friday 17 July, Aditi published a one-page plan. The squad would ship, in order: the fulfilment SLA view, the order-search fix, bulk label printing, the returns workflow at its reduced nine-week estimate, the webhook rebuild, and the third courier integration — 33 engineer-weeks. Split shipments, now at 16 weeks, went next, taking the committed total to 49 and leaving 17 weeks against the 66. Of that reserve, five weeks went to a read-only AI prototype answering five named operational questions, and twelve were held back for festive hardening and incidents.

Her reasoning, recorded in three lines at the foot of the page, was this. The ranking put cheap high-leverage work first because that maximised outcome per week against a hard freeze. The webhook rebuild was moved ahead of the courier integration despite a near-identical ratio because split shipments depended on it. And the AI prototype was funded not on its ratio, which was terrible, but out of an explicit exploration allocation — a decision made outside the ranking rather than by corrupting the scores to justify it. That last distinction is the mark of someone who understands the tool: the matrix tells you what the ratio says, and you are permitted to overrule it, in writing, for stated reasons.

What to learn next follows directly from the seams exposed here. RICE scoring decomposes the value axis into reach, impact and confidence, and is the natural next step once “everything is an 8” becomes a problem. Weighted scoring and WSJF generalise the numerator to several weighted criteria and introduce cost of delay, which is what you need when timing rather than size drives value. Kano analysis attacks the assumption that value is linear, distinguishing features whose absence is fatal from those whose presence delights. MoSCoW handles the non-negotiables the ratio cannot rank. And buy-a-feature is a way of extracting honest value estimates from customers who, like stakeholders, will otherwise tell you everything matters.

Two questions to sit with. First: in the last ranking you took part in, which single estimate, had it been wrong by half, would have changed the order — and did anyone check it? Second: if your team's ratio ordering were followed strictly for four consecutive quarters, what kind of product would you have at the end of it, and what would you never have built?

Value versus Effort

A full treatment of the two-by-two that every other prioritisation framework is a repair to: its mechanics, its formal limits, the schools that disagree about it, and the places where following it faithfully is the most expensive mistake available.

1. Two rooms, five weeks apart

On Monday 3 August 2026, in a converted textile-mill office off Ashram Road in Ahmedabad, Rohan Mistry pinned a sheet of butcher paper to the wall and wrote two numbers on it: 210 and 16. Rohan was VP Product at Lohit Freight Systems, which sold a transport-management platform to Indian fleet operators — route planning, e-way bill reconciliation, driver settlement — and also shipped its own telematics box, a ruggedised device bolted into the cab of a truck that reported location, fuel level and harsh-braking events. Lohit had 190 fleet customers running about 41,000 trucks, ₹96 crore of revenue, five product squads and a hardware team of nine.

The 210 was engineer-weeks available in the half-year to 31 January 2027. The 16 was weeks of lead time on the next-generation telematics board from Lohit's contract manufacturer. If Rohan wanted the new board in trucks before the March pre-monsoon fleet-renewal season, the bill of materials had to be frozen by 15 September — six weeks away — and frozen meant frozen: the decision to include or omit a CAN-bus reader, at ₹640 per unit across an expected 26,000 units, could not be revisited for fifteen months. The software items on his list could be re-sequenced any Monday. The hardware item could be decided once.

Five weeks later, on Wednesday 9 September, in a very different room on the fourth floor of an office in Koramangala, Bengaluru, Ira Deshmukh faced a list that looked similar and behaved nothing like it. Ira was group product manager at Lavanya Bazaar, a marketplace connecting neighbourhood kirana stores to regional packaged-food brands: 71,000 registered stores, 2,300 sellers, ₹1,480 crore of annualised GMV, take rate 3.1%. Her three squads had 96 engineer-weeks to the end of the December quarter and eleven candidate items, of which five served buyers — the store owners placing orders — and six served sellers, the brands and distributors filling them.

Ira's problem was that the two sides did not share a scale. A change that cut seller onboarding from nine days to three would raise catalogue breadth, which mattered only if buyers were currently leaving because they could not find what they wanted. A change that added a credit-terms display for buyers would raise order frequency, which mattered only if sellers could absorb the volume. Both items had value; the value of each was conditional on the other side being the binding constraint, and nobody in the room agreed about which side that was. A naive value-versus-effort ranking would have answered the question by averaging away the only thing worth arguing about.

These two decisions — an irreversible hardware commitment inside a reversible software plan, and a ranking across two populations whose values are coupled — are where the standard tool starts to creak. Both men and women in those rooms knew the tool. The question this page takes seriously is what an expert does when the tool's assumptions fail, and how to tell, before you have spent the quarter, that they have.

2. The idea, its history, and the four schools

Stated at its most careful: the value-versus-effort matrix is a device for allocating a fixed delivery budget across a set of candidate work items by estimating, for each, the expected contribution to a stated outcome within a stated horizon (value) and the total cost to reach a shippable state (effort), and sequencing so that the items with the highest ratio of the former to the latter are undertaken first. The two-dimensional plot is incidental. The ratio and the cut line are the substance.

Its ancestry is threefold. The oldest strand is operations research: the problem of choosing a subset of projects under a budget constraint is the knapsack problem, studied formally from the 1950s, and the ratio ordering is its classic greedy approximation, known to be near-optimal when individual items are small relative to the budget and to be arbitrarily bad when they are not. The second strand is the post-war quality movement — Kaoru Ishikawa's quality-control circles and the family of "seven management tools" that included a prioritisation matrix, which taught shop-floor teams to argue about placement rather than about conclusions. The third is strategy consulting: the Boston Consulting Group's growth–share matrix of 1970 made the two-by-two the standard grammar of resource allocation in large firms, and by the 1980s any manager could read one without instruction.

Software inherited all three. The impact–effort matrix appears in Lean and Agile practice through the 2000s. Donald Reinertsen's work on product-development flow, culminating in his 2009 book, replaced "value" with cost of delay — the economic loss per unit time from not having the thing — and argued that dividing cost of delay by duration produces a sequencing rule with a formal optimality property that raw value-over-effort does not have. That rule reached a wide audience as WSJF inside the Scaled Agile Framework. Intercom's RICE, published in 2016, attacked the other axis, decomposing value into reach, impact and confidence. Kano's model, from a 1984 paper by Noriaki Kano and colleagues, attacked the premise underneath both: that value is a continuous quantity at all.

There are, in practice, four positions on this terrain. They are not schools with buildings and journals, but they are recognisably different intellectual commitments, and competent practitioners genuinely hold each of them.

What unites all four is the premise that capacity is finite and that ordering matters. What divides them is what the numerator should be, whether the denominator is knowable, and whether features are the right things to be ranking. Rohan at Lohit was, without having named it, an economic-sequencing man: he thought in lead times and irreversible commitments. Ira at Lavanya Bazaar was pushed towards the threshold school by the structure of her market, because a marketplace with insufficient catalogue is not a worse marketplace, it is a non-functioning one.

3. Mechanics in depth

The version of the mechanic taught in most courses has three steps. The version experienced practitioners actually run has nine, and the four that separate them are the ones nobody writes down.

Step one: state the outcome and the horizon before you look at the list. A value estimate is a conditional forecast; it has no meaning without the condition. Rohan wrote: "Outcome to 31 January: renew 92% of fleet contracts by vehicle count, and win 4,000 new vehicles at or above ₹310 per vehicle per month." Every subsequent number on his sheet is an estimate of contribution to that sentence.

Step two: audit the candidate set. This is the first omitted step and the most consequential. The list you rank is the output of an unaudited filtering process: it contains what sales escalated, what support could articulate, and what engineers wanted to build. It does not contain what nobody thought of. Before ranking, an expert asks which of the three or four largest levers on the stated outcome has no item on the list at all. At Lohit, the answer was driver-app adoption, which drove renewal more strongly than any feature on the sheet and had been left off because no customer had "requested" it.

Step three: normalise the items to comparable size. The greedy ratio rule's approximation guarantee degrades as items grow relative to the budget. A practical rule: no item should exceed roughly one-sixth of the budget; anything larger should be split into a first increment that delivers standalone value and a remainder that is re-ranked later.

Step four: estimate value in units, not points, wherever units exist. Points compress and points get gamed. Rupees of revenue protected, rupees of cost avoided, or basis points of retention are harder to argue and easier to audit. Where units are genuinely unavailable — an exploratory item, a developer-experience improvement — say so explicitly and score it separately rather than inventing a spurious rupee figure.

Step five: estimate effort as a distribution, then calibrate. A single-point estimate discards the information that matters. Lohit's teams gave a ten-fiftieth-ninetieth percentile triple for each item, and Rohan applied a team-specific calibration multiplier derived from the previous two quarters. Lohit's platform squad had historically delivered at 1.45× its median estimate; the mobile squad at 1.1×. Applying the multiplier changes rankings, because it penalises large and unfamiliar work proportionally more than small and familiar work.

Step six: compute the ratio — and, where value decays with time, compute CD3 instead. CD3 is cost of delay divided by duration. The distinction is not pedantic. Two items can have identical total value and identical effort, and if one of them loses a third of its value every month it is not waiting, it must go first. The formal result underneath is a scheduling theorem: when jobs have linear delay costs, sequencing by delay-cost-per-unit-duration minimises total economic loss. This is the strongest formal claim anyone in this field can make, and it is a claim about sequencing, not about selection.

Step seven: fill capacity and locate the cut line. Step eight: run a sensitivity pass — for every item near the cut, compute the break-even input: the value at which it would drop below the line, or the effort at which it would. Step nine: record the deliberate overrides, with the reason and the person who owns each.
