Read the S row carefully, because it contains the whole argument for the economic-sequencing position. Item S — a pack of analytics that lets Lohit's account managers show a fleet operator, at renewal time, how much fuel the platform saved them — is worth ₹120 lakh a year, less than a third of the route optimiser. On a value-versus-effort chart it is a modest dot. But its value is almost entirely realised in a ten-week window, and if it ships in February the window has closed. Its cost of delay per month, ₹19 lakh, is nearly as high as the route optimiser's, whose value is smeared evenly across the year. Divide by the three weeks it takes and S is the single best use of Lohit's next three weeks by a wide margin. Plain value-over-effort put it second; it deserves to be first, and in a less careful shop it would have been fourth because "it's only analytics."

Second-order effects experts watch for

The first is Goodhart's problem applied to scores: as soon as a score determines whose work gets built, the score stops measuring value and starts measuring political skill. The observable tell is variance collapse — within two quarters of introducing a scoring system, every submitted item scores between 7 and 9. The second is the strategic use of effort estimates. Engineers who dislike a piece of work estimate it generously; engineers who want to build something estimate it tightly. Because the estimate sits in the denominator, a 40% shading of effort has a larger effect on rank than a 40% shading of value in a compressed value scale. The third is carrying cost: every shipped feature imposes a permanent tax — support load, test-suite time, migration burden on every future change. A team that ranks purely on delivery cost will, over eight quarters, accumulate a portfolio whose maintenance consumes the capacity that made the ranking worth doing. The fourth is queueing: capacity loaded above roughly 80% produces non-linear increases in cycle time, so the slack a plan leaves unallocated is not waste, it is purchased throughput. Filling 100% of 210 engineer-weeks is a prioritisation decision, and usually a bad one.

4. When it applies, and when it is actively misleading

The conditions under which ratio ranking is sound can be stated as testable claims rather than as cautions. Each can be checked in an afternoon.

Claim one: items are small relative to the budget. Test: is the largest item less than a sixth of capacity? At Lohit, the route optimiser at 54 weeks against 138 fails this badly, which is why Rohan's team enumerated the four feasible subsets by hand rather than trusting the sort. At Lavanya Bazaar, the largest item was 21 weeks against 96 — borderline, and Ira split it.

Claim two: item values are independent. Test: would the value of any item change materially if a different item shipped first? Lohit's fuel-theft alerting and the driver app share a telemetry pipeline; shipping the app first cuts the alerting item's effort by four weeks. That is a dependency, and dependencies make the sort invalid as written. At Lavanya Bazaar the coupling is worse: seller-side and buyer-side values are functions of each other.

Claim three: effort estimates are unbiased or calibratable. Test: do you have at least two quarters of estimate-versus-actual data by team? Lohit did. Many organisations discover, on looking, that they have never recorded an actual, which means their denominators are decorative.

Claim four: value is roughly linear in scope. Test: if you delivered half of this item, would you get roughly half the value? For the analytics pack, yes. For a compliance feature, emphatically no — half a mandated capability is worth zero and possibly negative. This is the Kano threshold objection in operational form.

Claim five: one decision-maker controls the capacity being allocated. Test: can you actually stop any item on the list? If three of the eleven are commitments made by a sales leader to a customer, they are not candidates and should be removed from the ranking and shown as fixed load, so that everyone sees what remains.

Where the idea is actively misleading — worse than no framework — is a shorter list, and it is worth naming precisely. First, irreversible decisions with option value: Rohan's CAN-bus reader is not a ranking problem, it is an options problem, and ratio arithmetic will systematically under-price the ability to do something later. Second, threshold work: latency, reliability, regulatory compliance, safety. Below the threshold the value of partial delivery is zero; above it, further delivery is nearly worthless. Third, enabling and platform work, whose value appears in other rows. Fourth, situations where the binding constraint is not capacity at all — if the team is blocked on a legal review or a partner integration, more work in the queue does not help and the ranking is answering a question nobody is facing.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Two-sided markets: Lavanya Bazaar's real problem

Ira's eleven items could not be ranked on one scale because value flowed to two populations whose satisfaction was coupled and whose constraint status changed over time. The approach her team settled on was to score each item twice — buyer value and seller value, each in expected incremental GMV — and then to apply a constraint weight determined empirically rather than by argument. The empirical question was: at the margin, what is stopping GMV from growing? Lavanya's data answered it: 38% of buyer searches returned fewer than three in-stock results, and seller-side fill rates were at 94%. Catalogue breadth, not seller capacity, was binding. Seller-side items therefore received a weight of 1.0 and buyer-side items a weight of 0.4 — not because buyers mattered less, but because buyer-side improvements would be throttled by an inventory shortage the buyer items did not address.

Hardware plus software: the irreversible row

Rohan's CAN-bus reader illustrates a structural problem. Its expected value was ₹210 lakh a year, mostly from a fuel-analytics upsell, and its incremental cost was ₹640 per unit, so at 26,000 units the direct cost was ₹166 lakh plus roughly eleven engineer-weeks of firmware. Ratio arithmetic makes it a middling item. But the ratio ignores two facts: that omitting it forecloses the fuel-analytics product for fifteen months, and that including it costs money whether or not the analytics ever ships. Mature hardware companies handle this by removing such items from the ranking altogether and treating them as option purchases with an explicit price and an explicit expiry — "we are paying ₹166 lakh for the right to launch fuel analytics in FY28" — and then asking whether that option is worth its price, which is a different and more honest question than where it sits on a list.

Regulated products

At Lavali Health Cloud, which sells clinical-documentation software to mid-sized hospital chains, roughly 30% of every release cycle goes to work mandated by regulation or by the certification bodies that hospital customers answer to — consent handling under India's data-protection regime, audit trails, retention rules. None of it is rankable. A mandated item at half scope is worth zero and may be worse than zero, because it creates the appearance of compliance. The mature practice is to take mandated work off the top as fixed load, publish the residual capacity, and rank only within that. Organisations that instead score compliance items and let them win on "value" end up with a ranking system whose top five rows are always the same, and whose credibility drains away because it never surprises anyone.

AI-native work

AI features break both axes at once. The effort distribution is wider than for conventional software — the gap between the tenth and ninetieth percentile is routinely 4:1 rather than 2:1, because whether a model reaches an acceptable quality bar is discovered rather than planned. And the value is conditional on a quality threshold that is itself uncertain: an assistant that answers correctly 82% of the time may be worth a great deal or nothing, depending on the cost of the 18%. The practice that works is to split the item into an evaluation increment — two to three weeks to build a test set and measure the achievable accuracy — and to make the rest of the item conditional on the result. Ranked as a whole, such an item almost always loses; ranked as a cheap information purchase followed by a conditional commitment, it often wins. There is also a denominator subtlety: inference cost is a recurring operational expense, so an AI feature's true cost includes a running charge that a one-time effort estimate does not capture.

Organisational seams

The gap between how mature companies describe their prioritisation and how they conduct it is widest at the seams between teams. Officially, a portfolio ranking allocates capacity to the highest-ratio work across the organisation. In practice, capacity is allocated by headcount, headcount is allocated annually, and each team ranks within a budget it cannot exchange with another team's. The consequence is that the organisation systematically funds the best item in each squad's local list rather than the best items overall — and the best available move is often to fund one squad's eighth-ranked item never, and give those weeks to another squad's third. Companies that do this well have a small quarterly forum with the authority to move perhaps 15% of capacity across team boundaries, and they treat that 15% as the only genuine portfolio decision they make.

6. Nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The diagonal, not the quadrant

Competent practitioners plot the grid and read the boxes. Experts read the slope from the origin, because that slope is the ratio, and the quadrant boundaries are arbitrary. Tell-tale sign: a team arguing about whether an item is "high effort" without reference to what it is being compared against. The obvious reading — that the four boxes carry meaning — is wrong because the midlines are set by whoever drew the chart.

Effort is a distribution, and the tail is where the quarter dies

Two items with the same median effort are not equivalent if one has a fat right tail. Experts rank on expected effort but plan on the ninetieth percentile of the two or three largest items, because those are the only ones that can consume a quarter. Tell-tale sign: an estimate given as a single confident number for work the team has never done before. The obvious reading — that a point estimate is a forecast — is wrong; it is usually the mode of a skewed distribution.

The numerator is usually cost of delay, not value

Most value is perishable to some degree; a great deal of it is sharply perishable. An expert asks of every item, "what does this cost us per month of delay?" and discovers that the ordering it implies differs from the value ordering for about a third of any real list. Tell-tale sign: an item whose annual value is modest but whose entire value sits inside a named window — a renewal cycle, a regulatory date, a festive season.

Score compression is a message about incentives

When every item scores 8, the problem is not that people cannot estimate; it is that scoring low is costly for the person submitting. Tell-tale sign: the standard deviation of value scores falling quarter on quarter. The obvious reading — that the team needs better training on the rubric — is wrong; the fix is to change what the score does, usually by force-ranking, by requiring units, or by separating the person who proposes from the person who scores.

Slack is a purchased good, not leftover

Queueing behaviour means that a team loaded to 100% of nominal capacity will deliver later and less predictably than one loaded to 80%, and the difference is non-linear near the top. An expert allocates 15–25% of capacity to nothing in particular and defends it as a throughput investment. Tell-tale sign: a plan whose committed effort exactly equals available capacity, which is always a sign that capacity was treated as a container to fill rather than as a system with dynamics.

Every shipped feature is a permanent liability

Carrying cost — support, test time, migration drag, cognitive load — accumulates silently and is never on the ranking sheet. An expert tracks the share of capacity consumed by maintenance and treats a rise in it as the delayed bill for previous rankings. Tell-tale sign: a team whose available engineer-weeks per quarter decline year on year while headcount is flat.

The candidate set is the decision, and nobody audits it

Ranking is a filter applied to a list someone else assembled, and the assembly process has its own biases: articulate customers, loud internal functions, engineers' interests. Tell-tale sign: a backlog in which every item traces to a request and none traces to a strategy. The obvious reading — that a well-run ranking produces good decisions — is wrong if the best available action was never a candidate.

Confidence is not always a multiplier

RICE's confidence factor works when outcomes are roughly continuous and the estimate is a mean. It fails for binary, large-consequence bets, where multiplying a huge payoff by 0.2 produces a number that flatters a gamble and disguises its variance. Tell-tale sign: a single item whose confidence-adjusted value exceeds the combined value of the next four. Such items should be funded in stages, not ranked.

Rank stability matters more than rank accuracy

Nobody needs to know whether an item is fourth or fifth; they need to know whether it is above or below the cut line. An expert spends estimation effort disproportionately on the three or four items nearest the line and almost none on the items obviously in or obviously out. Tell-tale sign: a team that re-estimates the whole backlog to two decimal places every quarter, which is precision spent where it cannot change a decision.

Ratio ordering has a documented failure pattern over long horizons

Because small items tend to have attractive ratios, strict adherence produces a product that improves continuously and never changes category. Tell-tale sign: four consecutive quarters in which every delivered item was under six weeks. The obvious reading — that the team is being efficient — is wrong; efficiency at the wrong altitude is how incumbents lose.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products, reach is the dominant term and it is measurable: the number of users who touch a surface can be counted, and a comparable past change gives a defensible impact prior. Value estimates are noisy but empirical, and — crucially — falsifiable afterwards through experiment. In B2B and enterprise, reach collapses. Ten accounts may represent half the revenue, so value becomes account-specific and the honest number is a retention or expansion figure attached to named customers. The discipline that distinguishes good B2B prioritisation is the requirement to state how many other accounts would use the same capability, with a number, before an escalation becomes a roadmap item.

In platforms and marketplaces the single-scale assumption fails structurally, as Lavanya Bazaar's case shows, and the honest practice is two scores and an evidenced constraint weight. In hardware, irreversibility and lead time dominate: the ranking question is subordinate to a scheduling question, because some decisions have expiry dates and others do not. In AI products, as described above, the distinctive move is to buy information cheaply before committing.

It is worth saying plainly where the difference is not real, because a good deal of published advice manufactures distinctions. The arithmetic is identical everywhere. The failure modes — score compression, optimistic effort, quadrant theatre, neglected enabling work — are identical everywhere, and they appear in a seven-person startup and in a 4,000-person firm in the same proportions. What changes is which of the tool's assumptions fails first, and how expensive it is when it does.

Stage changes the reliability of each axis in opposite directions. Early, effort estimates are good, because the estimator does the work and the system is small; value estimates are close to guesses, because there is no history and no base rate. The ranking exercise at that stage is mostly useful for exposing that half the list serves no live outcome. Late, value estimates improve — enough customers, enough past releases, enough measurement — while effort estimates degrade, because of cross-team dependencies, release trains, compliance review and the carrying cost of a decade of features. The mature-company pathology is therefore not bad value estimation but systematic effort underestimation, which biases the portfolio towards ambitious work that does not finish.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Example one: Rohan's subset enumeration

Because Lohit's largest item violated the small-items condition, Rohan did not trust the sort. With 138 allocatable weeks after a 72-week reserve for incidents, hardware support and the fixed compliance load, he enumerated the feasible subsets. Taking the ratio order — Q (16), S (9), P (28), R (20), U (11) — consumes 84 weeks for ₹1,025 lakh of annual value, leaving 54 weeks, exactly enough for T. Total: ₹1,445 lakh across all six. Alternatively, starting with T (54) and then taking the ratio order until the budget is exhausted gives the same set. In this instance the constraint was not binding and the greedy answer was also the optimal one — but Rohan only knew that because he checked, and the check took twenty minutes. Had the reserve been larger, at 110 allocatable weeks, the greedy order would have delivered Q, S, P, R, U = 84 weeks and ₹1,025 lakh with 26 weeks stranded, while dropping R and U (₹285 lakh, 31 weeks) would not have freed enough for T either. The genuinely optimal move at 110 weeks was the greedy set plus deliberately unallocated time, not a heroic attempt to squeeze T in at reduced scope.

Example two: Ira's weighted two-sided ranking

That last sentence is the point of the example. The weighting concentrates the entire decision into one empirical claim — that supply, not demand, is binding — and makes it fragile in a useful way. Ira wrote the claim on the first line of the plan with the three pieces of evidence supporting it and a re-test date of 15 January. That is a considerably more honest artefact than a single-scale ranking in which the same assumption would have been made implicitly and never written down.

Example three: where it failed — Lohitaksh Payments

Lohitaksh Payments built collection and reconciliation software for small merchants. Between FY23 and FY25 the company ran a disciplined value-versus-effort process every quarter, and by any internal measure it worked: delivery predictability rose, stakeholder complaints fell, and the team shipped between fourteen and nineteen items a quarter against a plan.

What went wrong is instructive because nothing went wrong procedurally. Ratio ranking favours small items; small items are, almost by construction, improvements to what exists; and a portfolio of improvements to what exists is exactly the wrong response to a competitor who has changed the architecture. The new entrant had built automatic bank-feed reconciliation, a nine-month platform investment that would never have survived a quarterly ratio ranking at any point in its life, because its value was zero until the last month of it and its effort exceeded a quarter's capacity. The column that shows the damage is "items over 8 weeks": it went to zero and stayed there, which is the clearest early warning sign in this entire page.

Recovery took five quarters and looked like this. Lohitaksh split its capacity into three books with separate governance: 60% to ranked incremental work, 25% to a single named multi-quarter bet with milestone funding rather than a ratio, and 15% to platform health with a floor that could not be raided. It re-founded the ranking process on cost of delay rather than raw value, which immediately raised the priority of several items whose value was concentrated in the GST filing calendar. And it instituted a quarterly question with teeth: "what is the largest item we have declined in each of the last four quarters, and is it the same one?" A recurring decline is the fingerprint of work that a ratio cannot justify and a strategy requires. By FY27 H1 retention had recovered to 103%, though win rate against the entrant remained below its FY24 level — which is the honest ending, because architectural ground once ceded is not usually recovered by better prioritisation.

9. Failure modes, warning signs, and the cost of catching them late

Score compression. Early sign: falling variance in the value column; every request an 8. Diagnostic question: "If we could only do one of these two, which goes?" asked pairwise on the top six. Cost of catching it late: moderate and recoverable — a quarter of effort spent on the wrong ordering, with most of the value still available afterwards.

Systematic effort underestimation. Early sign: the ratio of actual to estimated effort exceeds 1.3 for two consecutive quarters, and is worse for larger items. Diagnostic question: "What did the last three items of this size actually cost, including migration and support enablement?" Cost of catching it late: high, because the bias is directional — it inflates the apparent attractiveness of large ambitious work, so the damage compounds into a portfolio of unfinished big things.

Enabling work starvation. Early sign: the proportion of capacity going to platform, tooling and data infrastructure falls below about 10% for three quarters, while cycle time for a standard item rises. Diagnostic question: "Has the effort estimate for a typical medium feature increased over the last year?" Cost of catching it late: very high. Recovery requires a rebuild that is itself unrankable, which is how teams end up in a two-year platform programme they cannot justify to anyone.

Incrementalism lock-in. Early sign: no shipped item exceeded eight weeks for four consecutive quarters, as at Lohitaksh. Diagnostic question: "What is the largest item we have declined repeatedly, and what would have to be true for it to be right?" Cost of catching it late: the highest on this list, and frequently not recoverable, because by the time it is visible in retention a competitor has a two-year architectural lead.

Constraint drift in two-sided products. Early sign: the weighting between sides has not been re-derived from data in more than two quarters. Diagnostic question: "What evidence would tell us the other side is now binding, and when did we last look at it?" Cost of catching it late: high — an entire year of capacity applied to a side that stopped being the bottleneck, usually visible only as unexplained flatness in the aggregate metric.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether effort should be estimated at all. The estimation-sceptic position, in its strongest form, is not laziness: it observes that estimate error in most organisations is large and biased, that the act of estimating consumes real capacity, and that measured cycle-time distributions for uniformly sliced work predict delivery better than any estimate the same team produces. Its evidence is empirical — flow data from teams that abandoned estimation and did not get worse. For it to be wrong, it would have to be the case that items cannot be sliced to a uniform size without destroying their coherence, which is plainly true for hardware, for migrations and for anything with a regulatory scope that cannot be delivered in parts. The steelman of the opposing view is that the denominator is doing real work even when it is inaccurate, because it forces a conversation about scope that otherwise never happens.

Whether value is continuous. The Kano-descended position holds that treating a must-have and a delighter as points on one scale is a category error, and its evidence is the repeated observation that customers do not trade off basic attributes against exciting ones — they disqualify products that fail on basics regardless of how attractive everything else is. For this to be wrong, it would have to be the case that thresholds are rare or that they can be approximated adequately by very high value scores. The opposing steelman is that in practice a threshold item can be handled by removing it from the ranking as fixed load, which preserves the simplicity of one scale for everything that remains — and that inventing a second taxonomy for every backlog costs more than it returns.

Whether cost of delay is estimable in practice. The economic-sequencing school insists that a rupee-per-week figure, even a rough one, dominates any points-based scheme because it has units and can be checked. Its critics respond that outside a few clean cases — a regulatory deadline, a seasonal window, a contract clause — cost of delay is a fabrication dressed in currency, and that the false precision is more dangerous than honest ordinal ranking. For the critics to be wrong, organisations would have to demonstrate that their cost-of-delay estimates were subsequently borne out, and very few have published such evidence. Both camps agree on the narrower claim: where value is demonstrably time-boxed, ignoring it is indefensible.

Whether features are the right unit at all. The outcome-first position holds that a well-run feature ranking is an efficient way to execute someone else's bad idea, and that capacity should be allocated to problems with measurable targets. Its evidence is the pattern visible at Lohitaksh: a process that optimised everything it could see while the thing that mattered was invisible to it. For it to be wrong, it would have to be the case that teams given outcomes without a candidate list mostly fail to generate good candidates — which is exactly what critics observe in organisations without strong discovery practice, and which is why the position is more defensible in some firms than in others. This is the disagreement least likely to be settled, because the right answer genuinely depends on the capability of the teams involved.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this material produces a well-formatted table and defends its conclusions. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in five observable ways. They spend most of their estimation effort on the two or three items nearest the cut line and refuse to refine the rest. They can state, without looking, which single assumption their current plan is most sensitive to and what would falsify it. They remove items from the ranking rather than forcing everything onto one scale — mandated work as fixed load, irreversible commitments as priced options, large architectural bets as milestone-funded programmes outside the ratio. They treat the ranking as a living function of inputs and hold a short standing session to ask what has been learned about those inputs. And they notice the shape of the portfolio over years, not just the order within a quarter, because the most expensive prioritisation mistakes are invisible inside any single quarter's arithmetic.

There is a sixth, subtler marker. A master of this tool is comfortable overruling it in public and in writing. The point of the ratio is not to remove judgement; it is to make judgement visible and expensive to exercise casually. An override recorded as "we are funding the route optimiser despite a CD3 of 1.4 because the alternative is conceding multi-depot accounts for two years, and we accept that this costs us roughly ₹90 lakh of nearer-term value" is a better artefact than any ranking, because it can be revisited and judged.

12. What they decided

On 15 September Rohan froze the bill of materials with the CAN-bus reader, and recorded the decision as an option purchase: ₹166 lakh for the right to launch fuel analytics in FY28, expiring in fifteen months, to be reviewed at the FY27 half-year with a named owner. His software plan followed the CD3 order — S, Q, P, R, U — for the first 84 weeks, with the route optimiser funded as a milestone programme with a scope review at week six rather than as a ranked item, and 72 weeks held as reserve and fixed load. He also added the driver-app adoption work that the candidate audit had surfaced, funding it from the exploration allocation rather than by inventing a value score for it.

Ira committed the top six weighted items, wrote the supply-constraint claim and its three pieces of evidence at the head of the plan, and set 15 January as the date on which the weights would be re-derived. She declined the buyer credit-terms item — the highest raw-value item on her sheet — and wrote down what would change her mind: if in-stock search coverage rose above 85% and seller capacity utilisation approached 80%, the weights would flip and credit terms would move to first.

Three questions in the manner of a teaching note. First: Rohan's option purchase and Ira's constraint weight are both devices for taking a decision out of the ranking — under what conditions does removing items from a ranking improve a decision, and when does it simply hide a preference? Second: Lohitaksh's process satisfied every quality criterion in this page except one, and still destroyed the business's position — if you had been its head of product in FY24 H1, what specific evidence available at that time should have changed the plan, and what would it have cost to act on it? Third: the estimation-sceptic and economic-sequencing schools disagree about whether the denominator is knowable — in your own organisation, what would you have to measure for six months to settle that question empirically, and why has nobody done it?

13. Going deeper

  1. Scoping the MVP — the first place value and effort are ranked against each other in anger; it teaches you that scope is an input to the effort estimate, not a fixed given, which is the single most useful lever in any ranking.
  2. Feature and prioritisation rationale — the discipline of recording why, which converts a ranking into an auditable decision and makes overrides reviewable rather than mysterious.
  3. RICE scoring — decomposes the value axis into reach, impact and confidence; the natural next step when score compression makes a single value number useless.
  4. Weighted scoring and WSJF — generalises the numerator to several weighted criteria and formalises cost of delay divided by duration; where the sequencing theorem in section 3 comes from.
  5. Buy-a-feature — a method for extracting honest value estimates from customers by forcing them to spend a constrained budget, which is the same knapsack in a room with stakeholders.
  6. MoSCoW and must-have analysis — handles the non-negotiables the ratio cannot rank, and gives you the vocabulary for taking mandated work off the top as fixed load.
  7. Kano model — the strongest challenge to the assumption that value is continuous; teaches you to separate basics, performance attributes and delighters before ranking anything.
  8. User story mapping — produces a candidate set organised by user journey rather than by request, which directly addresses the unaudited-backlog problem in section 3.
  9. Prioritising under constraints — the formal treatment of dependencies, fixed dates and capacity limits, including the subset enumeration Rohan ran when the small-items condition failed.
  10. Saying no — the interpersonal half of the work; a ranking that nobody can enforce is a document, and the enforcement is where most prioritisation systems actually fail.
  11. Strategic themes and outcome-based prioritisation — the outcome-first school's positive programme, and the antidote to the Lohitaksh pattern of efficient incrementalism.
  12. Cost of delay — the deepest of the follow-ons; make the numerator an economic quantity with units and most of the arguments in this page become arithmetic rather than opinion.
